cards.name: Inspirational / motivational
cards.summary: Optimistic, forward-looking copy that shows the reader what is possible and that they can reach it. Good inspirational writing is anchored in one real person, number or moment and ends on a small, doable first step, never on a poster quote.
use_for: motivational speeches, keynotes and TED-style talks
brand manifestos and founder or CEO letters
crowdfunding and fundraising pages that need the reader to believe a change is possible
Instagram and LinkedIn posts about a customer or founder turning point
recruitment ads and college essays that show growth
avoid: Poster-quote filler ('believe in yourself', 'dream big', 'the sky is the limit'): replace each with one specific person, number or moment that proves it.

Pep aimed at a reader who is confused, new or hurting: Atlassian's guidance is to be less optimistic when the reader feels unsupported or uncertain, so drop the volume and give the first small step (see tone:empathetic_supportive).
Outcome promises ('you will earn Rs 1 lakh a month'): show the process and what it cost the person instead; income and results claims are a compliance matter.
Toxic positivity that skips the obstacle: name the obstacle in one clause, then the way through.
Stacked superlatives, several exclamation marks, and send-offs such as 'the future looks bright': they read as AI filler and the PCW check flags them.
markers: NN/g position (the harvest's placement on NN/g's four dimensions): enthusiastic rather than matter-of-fact, ranging from light to serious with the stakes, respectful.
Opens with a person, a number or a concrete moment (a name, a town, a date), not with a slogan.
One proof point per paragraph; every uplifting claim has a fact next to it within two sentences.
Second person ('you') for the invitation, 'we' only at the turn when the writer stands with the reader.
Verbs of starting and moving (start, build, begin, reach, ship); concrete nouns (a stove, a stall, a phone), few abstract ones (potential, excellence).
Short declarative sentences at the turn; at most one rule-of-three list in the piece.
At most one exclamation mark per piece; no emoji stacks (one or two in a Hinglish caption is fine).
Optimism scaled to the reader: more for ambitious readers, less and more practical for new or uncertain ones.
Ends on a first step the reader can do today (do this, by when), not on a moral.
cards.sample: Sunita Devi sold her first forty jars of achar from a Bhilwara kitchen. Last month she shipped three thousand to Dubai. She had no MBA, no website, no loan. She had a stove, her mother-in-law's recipe and a phone with WhatsApp. If one kitchen can reach Dubai, your idea can reach its next customer. Start smaller than you think you should. Start with your first forty.

sources.title: Atlassian Design System: Voice and tone
sources.supports: 'optimistic' voice trait: be more optimistic for readers who feel ambitious, inspired or curious and less for readers who feel unsupported, confused or uncertain

cards.name: Irreverent / edgy
cards.summary: Pokes at conventions, authority or the category itself and is deliberately not polite. It works only when the target is an idea or a habit the reader already finds silly, and when a real product fact sits under the joke.
use_for: brand and social copy for a challenger D2C, fintech or media brand
taglines, banners and OOH that mock the category's clichés
meme captions and sponsored creator posts for a young, online audience
topical posts and moment marketing that need a cheeky stance
sketch and stand-up material that mocks conventions
avoid: Aiming the joke at the reader or customer: NN/g notes irreverent tones are usually irreverent about the subject matter, not the audience. Aim at the category, the jargon, the ritual.
Edge with no claim underneath ('we're not like other brands'): put one hard product fact in the second line so the stance has something to stand on.
Mocking religion, caste, gender, disability or a named real person: out of bounds for paid client work; check the compliance cards.
Irreverence in error, grief, health or money-loss moments: switch to calm, plain copy.
Shock words as padding: one sharp line beats five coarse ones.
markers: NN/g position: irreverent pole of respectful-irreverent, normally paired with casual and funny (the NN/g playful samples sit at funny, casual, irreverent, enthusiastic).
Opens by taking a stance in the first line ('Branded chai at Rs 180 a cup.'), not by greeting the reader.
A named, specific target: the category's cliché, a corporate phrase, a ritual ('artisanal single-origin'), not 'other brands'.
Short sentences and fragments; contractions; the punchline is the last word of the line.
Understatement or deadpan after the jab; no explaining the joke.
Direct address is allowed but never an insult ('you' is the one in on the joke).
No swearing and no slurs unless the client's voice guide explicitly allows mild language.
Exclamation marks are rare; the edge comes from word choice, not volume.
cards.sample:
Single-origin, small-batch, hand-poured, Rs 180 a cup.
The chaiwala outside our office does it for Rs 15 and has never once said 'terroir'.
We still think premium chai is a good idea. We just think it should taste better than the story told about it. Ours does. 100 g, Assam, Rs 249. Judge us after the first cup.

cards.name: Journalistic neutral
cards.summary: Reports what happened and who said what, from nobody's point of view: attribution over adjectives, one verifiable fact per sentence. Neutral does not mean equal weight for a claim the evidence does not support.
use_for: hard news stories, live blogs and video bulletin scripts
news explainers and fact-checks that must stay fair to all sides
photo captions, event recaps and headline-plus-dek copy
government press notes and press releases that report facts without adjectives
documentary narration that states, not preaches
avoid: False balance: giving a fringe claim and a well-evidenced claim equal space is not neutral. Say what the evidence supports and attribute the rest.
Loaded verbs and adjectives ('slammed', 'blasted', 'shocking', 'controversial'): use 'said', 'told', 'according to' and the number or fact instead.
Unattributed claims and opinion dressed as fact: every contested statement names who said it, with role and date.
Editorialising in the headline or the last paragraph: if the piece needs a view, label it opinion or analysis and move it out of the news text.
Quoting only one side: record who was asked and did not respond, in a plain sentence.
markers: Position on the NN/g dimensions (inferred, not stated by a source): serious, matter-of-fact, respectful, neutral formality.
'Said' as the default speech verb; no 'claimed', 'admitted', 'revealed' unless the fact itself is the claim.
First mention gives full name and role; later mentions use surname or role only.
Third person throughout; no 'we', no 'I', no direct address; no rhetorical questions.
One fact per sentence, short enough that the attribution sits in the same sentence; numbers carry their source and date ('according to the 2024 survey').
Past tense for events; present tense for standing facts and for what a source says is still true.
Adjectives only when they are part of the record (a 40-year-old bridge), never as judgement.
Direct quotes are verbatim and attributed in the same sentence; paraphrase is used for the rest.
Opinion or analysis is labelled as such.
cards.sample: The Shivpur Nagar Parishad said on Monday that 38 of its 75 wards will get piped water by March 2027. Ward 12 councillor Rekha Kumari said residents have relied on tanker water since 2023. In a written statement, the parishad's executive engineer said pipe-laying along the main market road had delayed the work. The state urban development department did not respond to questions sent on Sunday.

sources.title: Journalistic objectivity (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: objectivity = truthfulness, neutrality and detachment; a known failure is false balance between unequal claims

cards.name: Kid-friendly
cards.summary: Short, concrete, warm sentences a child can follow, without talking down. One idea per sentence, things the child can see or do, and no irony.
use_for: children's picture-book and story text
kids' explainers, lesson scripts, quizzes and e-learning modules
comic, audio-series and game dialogue for young players
packaging and PSAs aimed at children or at parents reading aloud
subtitles and on-screen text for children's programmes
avoid: Talking down: baby talk, 'simply', 'it's easy', 'even you can'. Google's tone guide flags condescending phrasing; speak to the child as a capable small person.
Sarcasm and irony: children read them literally. Say the plain thing.
Scary urgency or fear hooks ('before it's too late'): use a calm, curious opener instead.
Abstract nouns and long clauses ('conservation of resources'): swap for something visible ('the tap keeps running, the tank gets empty').
Treating the child as a buyer: advertising to children has its own rules, handled in the compliance cards.
markers: Sentences are short: most carry one idea and fit on a single breath when read aloud.
Concrete, visible nouns (bus, dadi, bucket, rain); few abstract nouns; one new word at a time, explained by something familiar.
Active verbs and simple tenses; positive instructions ('hold the rail') rather than a list of don'ts.
Sound words and repetition (tap, plop, dhak-dhak) give rhythm and help memory.
Questions put to the child ('What do you think she did next?'), then answered in the next line.
Named characters with a feeling the child recognises (scared, proud, curious).
Warm but not sugary: no exclamation mark on every line, no stacked emoji.
On-screen text for children gets more time: Netflix's timed-text guide allows up to 17 characters per second for children's programmes against 20 for adults.
cards.sample: छोटी बूँद बादल से गिरी। टप! वह पहाड़ पर गिरी। टप! अब वह नदी में थी। नदी बहती रही, बहती रही। बूँद ने पूछा, “हम कहाँ जा रहे हैं?” नदी हँसी, “समुद्र के पास!” बूँद ने आँखें बंद कर लीं। उसे डर नहीं लगा। उसके साथ हज़ारों बूँदें थीं।

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: children's programmes get a slower reading speed (up to 17 characters per second vs 20 for adults)

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: voice and tone
sources.supports: conversational, friendly, respectful tone like a knowledgeable friend; avoid jargon, exclamation marks, figurative language, 'please' in steps, and condescending words such as 'simply' and 'it's easy'

cards.name: Luxury / premium
cards.summary: Restrained, assured and exclusive: craft, material, rarity and heritage stated plainly, never discounts or shouting. The price and the prestige are implied by what is left out.
use_for: product descriptions and catalogues for jewellery, fashion, watches, interiors and spirits
brand stories and about pages of premium and heritage-craft brands
hotel, resort and premium real-estate listings
print ads, packaging and wedding invitations
D2C store copy for a high-ticket collection
avoid: Discount and urgency language ('offer', 'sale', 'hurry', 'only 3 left'): it cheapens the brand. Use invitation language ('by appointment', 'reserve', 'available in 25 editions') and only when it is true.
Adjective stacks ('exquisite, stunning, luxurious'): luxury does not announce itself. Replace three adjectives with one fact (hours of work, material, origin, edition size).
Unverifiable superlatives ('the world's finest'): give the checkable detail instead.
Exclamation marks, all caps, emoji and slang: they break the register.
Snobbery that insults the reader: stay assured, not superior.
markers: Names the craft, material and origin precisely (Kundan, mulberry silk, Jaipur) with a process detail or a count that is true.
Very few adjectives; nouns and verbs carry the copy.
Calm, medium-short sentences; full stops, no exclamation marks, no emoji, no hashtags in the body.
Scarcity stated as a fact (an edition of 25, made to order in six weeks) rather than as a countdown.
No price pressure words: no 'cheap', 'deal', 'offer', 'discount', 'budget'; price is stated plainly or left to the enquiry.
Third person or a quiet 'we'; 'you' used sparingly and as a guest, not a target.
Sensory words used with restraint (weight, drape, patina, grain).
Personalisation and presentation treated as part of the product (monogram, packaging), in line with how luxury brands create exclusivity.
cards.sample: Kundan, set the way it has been set in Jaipur for generations. Each necklace takes eleven days. The gold foil is beaten by hand, the stones are fixed one at a time, and the enamel on the reverse is finished for no one but the wearer. Made in editions of twenty-five. Not discounted, not repeated. Viewings by appointment.

sources.title: Luxury goods (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: luxury brands communicate being top of their class; personalisation, special packaging and limited supply create exclusivity

cards.name: Minimalist / understated
cards.summary: The fewest words that carry the claim: plain statements, specifications instead of adjectives, white space around them. It lets the product or fact speak and only works when the fact underneath is strong.
use_for: taglines, billboards, banners and social bios
product pages and packaging for design-led or premium products
UX microcopy, push notifications and onboarding screens
release notes and homepage hero lines
link-in-bio and profile copy
avoid: Understatement over a weak claim: it just reads empty. Make sure one hard fact (a spec, a number, a proof) is on the page.
Cutting the words that carry the reader's next step (price, date, CTA, safety information): prune excess words, never the action.
Cryptic fragments the reader must decode: a fragment is fine when its meaning is obvious from the line above.
Cold or curt copy in an error or empathy moment: keep it short but add one human word.
Confusing minimal with vague ('Simply better'): replace with what is better and by how much.
markers: NN/g position: matter-of-fact (the opposite pole to enthusiastic), serious to dry, formality set by the brand.
Microsoft's crisp-and-clear principle: bigger ideas, fewer words; prune every excess word; short sentences and fragments.
One claim per line; keep each line short enough to read at a glance; line breaks do the work of paragraphs.
Specs, numbers and units instead of adjectives ('192 pages, 100 gsm', not 'premium quality paper').
No intensifiers (very, really, truly, extremely), no exclamation marks, no emoji; sentence case.
Plain everyday words; verbs in the active voice; articles dropped only where the meaning stays clear.
Full stops used for rhythm; one-line paragraphs allowed.
Humour, if any, is dry and single-line.
cards.sample:
Notebook No. 3.
192 pages. 100 gsm. Stitched, not glued.
Opens flat. Takes a fountain pen without bleeding.
Made in Noida.
Rs 349.
That is all it does.

sources.title: Microsoft Style Guide: brand voice
sources.supports: crisp and clear voice: bigger ideas and fewer words; prune every excess word; short sentences and fragments; short everyday words and contractions

cards.name: Nostalgic
cards.summary: Evokes a shared past (childhood, a decade, old India) to create warmth and belonging. It runs on specific sensory details of a period, not on the phrase 'good old days'.
use_for: brand stories and TVC or video-ad scripts for heritage or comfort products (mithai, drinks, biscuits, stationery)
festival and greeting copy that revives a family ritual
Instagram and social ad copy aimed at a 'millennial and 90s kids' cohort
personal essays, wedding speeches and vote-of-thanks that recall shared years
event promotion for reunions and throwback editions
avoid: Generic 'good old days' lines: swap in one specific object, sound, price or ritual of the period (a Rs 2 candy, a landline with a curly wire).
Anachronism: an object from the wrong decade breaks the spell for the very cohort you are courting. Check the year against the audience's birth years.
Mocking the present to praise the past: keep the warmth, drop the sneer.
Using painful history (Partition, the Emergency, riots) as a mood device: leave it out unless the brief is about it.
Ending in the past: bring it to the product or the offer in the last two lines.
markers: NN/g lists 'Nostalgic' as a tone word; it does not place it on the four dimensions, so treat it as warm, casual-to-formal depending on brand, and enthusiastic only in a gentle way.
Concrete period details: named objects, sounds, smells, prices, rituals ('chaarpai on the roof', 'the ring of a cycle bell').
Memory prompts in the second person ('yaad hai?', 'Remember the...'), then a bridge from then to now.
Short fragments for memory beats; one slightly longer sentence for the turn.
Past tense for the scene, present tense for the bridge to the product.
Kinship and place words in Hindi or Hinglish where native (Nani, gully, chhat, mohalla).
A slower rhythm than hype copy: fewer exclamation marks, no stacked emoji.
One concrete link from the memory to what is on offer.
cards.sample: Bijli gayi. Chaarpai chhat pe aa gayi. Kisi ne antakshari shuru ki, kisi ne aam kaat diye. Nobody checked a phone, because the only phone hung on the wall with a long, curly wire. This monsoon, bring that evening back. Aam panna, the way Nani made it: raw mango, roasted jeera, black salt, nothing else.

sources.title: Tone-of-Voice Words (NN/g)
sources.supports: 'Nostalgic' is one of NN/g's 37 tone words

cards.name: Playful / witty
cards.summary: Light, clever and fun: wordplay and one good surprise without losing the message. The joke carries the product fact, and clarity always wins over entertainment.
use_for: Instagram captions, social ads and X posts for lifestyle and D2C brands
push notifications, empty states and success messages in apps
taglines, packaging and product descriptions with personality
promotional emails and welcome series that need warmth
meme-style content where the humour is mild
avoid: Humour in serious industries: NN/g's study found humorous copy hurt credibility, with participants saying friendliness took credibility away. Use plain, calm copy for finance, health and legal.
Forcing a joke: Mailchimp's rule is to keep a straight face when unsure, because forced humour is worse than none.
Jokes in health, money-loss, grief, delay or error states: the reader is not in the mood; use tone:calm_reassuring instead.
A pun that hides the offer: if the reader cannot say what is being sold after the joke, rewrite so the fact comes first.
Dated meme slang and in-jokes only the team understands.
markers: NN/g position: funny, casual, irreverent-leaning, enthusiastic (the NN/g playful samples sit exactly there).
One joke or surprise per short paragraph, not a joke per sentence (rule of thumb).
The punchline is the last word of the line; set-up first, twist last.
Wordplay that also carries the product fact (a pun on the product's actual benefit), not a pun for its own sake.
Contractions, everyday words and short sentences; Hinglish where the audience speaks it.
Dry understatement is as valid as exclamation: Mailchimp prefers 'winking to shouting'.
At most one exclamation mark per piece; emoji sparingly, as seasoning.
Message first: the offer, date or action stays clear even if the reader misses the joke.
cards.sample: Our filter coffee decoction is strong enough to make Monday apologise. 250 ml, one spoon, hot milk. No whistle, no waiting, no 'five more minutes'. Okay, maybe five more minutes. Pune delivery in two days, because your couch is not going to deliver itself.

cards.name: Rebellious challenger brand
cards.summary: Names the status quo or the category's old habit as the enemy and positions the brand as the break-out. The enemy is a practice or a convention; the proof is a real difference in the product.
use_for: brand manifestos and positioning statements for an underdog brand
homepage and landing-page hero copy that leads with a stance
comparison and 'alternative to' pages (routed through compliance)
OOH, print and video ads that attack a category cliché
brand-story copy for a founder-led disruptor
avoid: Naming and disparaging a competitor without substantiation: comparative claims about a named rival are a compliance matter (see comp:trade_marks_comparative_ads and comp:asci_code). Attack the practice ('refined oil ads with a smiling family') not the brand.
A rebel pose over a me-too product: if there is no real difference, there is nothing to rebel with. Put the differentiator (an ingredient, a price, a lab report, a policy) in the second line.
Spending the whole piece on the enemy: say more about what you do than about what you oppose.
Sneering at customers who buy the incumbent: they are who you want to win.
Shouting: the stance is carried by specifics and short sentences, not capitals and exclamation marks.
markers: NN/g position: irreverent pole of respectful-irreverent, casual, enthusiastic; archetype: the Outlaw (Mark and Pearson).
Opens with the enemy as a plain statement of how things are done ('Half a century of the same oil ad.').
A 'they / we' contrast: they do X, we do Y, each with one proof point.
Belief statements in the first person plural ('We think you should see the lab report before you pay').
Short declarative sentences; fragments for the turn; contractions.
The enemy is a convention, a jargon word or a habit; a named competitor appears only when compliance has cleared it.
Concrete contrast pairs with numbers, places or documents the reader can check.
Ends with an invitation to switch, with the first step spelled out.
cards.sample: Cooking-oil ads have run the same film for fifty years: a smiling family and a bottle. We don't have a family. We have an oil, cold-pressed in Erode, and a lab report for every batch that you can read before you pay. The big labels sell you a smile. We'd rather show you the number. Scan the batch code on the bottle and read it.

cards.name: Regal / heritage
cards.summary: The stately, legacy-proud voice of an old house, a royal craft or a long tradition. Its authority comes from real dates, names and places, so the heritage must be true and checkable.
use_for: brand stories and about pages of heritage houses (handloom, jewellery, perfumery, sweets, hospitality)
catalogues, brochures and print ads for craft and heritage products
wedding and event invitation wording
annual-report narrative and CEO letters of legacy institutions
hotel and restaurant copy for palaces, havelis and old kitchens
avoid: Invented or inflated heritage ('since time immemorial', 'royal' with no royal link, a founding year nobody can document): it is a false claim. Use the real year, the real family or town, and the real process.
Stiff, archaic words that no reader uses ('hereinafter', 'be pleased to note'): formal does not mean dead; use clear, dignified sentences.
Heritage with no relevance today: show the tradition continuing in this year's product, or the piece reads as a museum label.
Over-ornament (every noun wearing an adjective): keep the register stately by being exact, not by decorating.
Slang, emoji and exclamation marks: they puncture the tone.
markers: NN/g position (harvest placement): formal, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact. NN/g's own tone words nearby: 'Conservative', 'Nostalgic'. Archetype: the Ruler (Mark and Pearson).
Heritage claims anchored in dates, places and names ('founded in 1923 in Lucknow'), each of which the client can document.
Full, well-formed sentences; third person for the house; longer sentences are welcome if the rhythm is steady.
Present-perfect continuity: 'has been woven since', 'remains', 'continues' to join past and present.
Dignified vocabulary: lineage, craft, atelier, house, generations; in Hindi, Sanskritised or Urdu-influenced words (विरासत, परंपरा, कारीगर, शाही) used naturally.
Capitalised proper nouns for the house, the craft and the region.
No slang, no emoji, no exclamation marks, no discount language.
Confidence expressed through facts (process, count, years), not through 'the finest'.
cards.sample: In Banaras, the loom has not fallen silent since before the brothers who tend it were born. Every sari begins as raw mulberry silk and a drawing in a notebook handed down from their grandfather. A brocade takes forty days. It is woven to be inherited, and each one carries the house's mark on the inside of the pallu.

cards.name: Romantic
cards.summary: A tender, intimate, longing voice for love, weddings, gifting and shayari-style captions. It is built from small, specific moments and soft rhythm, not from the word 'love'.
use_for: shayari, couplets and Valentine or anniversary captions
wedding invitation wording, wedding speeches and toasts
greeting and wishes messages for partners
gifting copy for jewellery, flowers, chocolates and personalised products
love scenes and dialogue in short stories, serials and micro-dramas
avoid: Stock imagery (rose, chand-sitare, 'my soulmate', 'you complete me'): swap for one small shared moment (cutting chai, a rain-stuck auto, her dupatta on his shoulder).
Over-sweet stacks of superlatives: one image per line is plenty.
Explicit or overfamiliar language in a family or wedding setting: keep it tender and respectful of the audience.
Using romance as a sales lever with pressure ('last day to show you love'): the gift can be the proof of attention, not a deadline.
Slang ('bae') or a flip register in a formal wedding piece.
markers: NN/g lists 'Romantic' as a tone word without placing it on the four dimensions; treat it as warm, personal, and light-to-serious by occasion.
Intimate person: 'main/tum' or 'I/you', speaking to one person, not to an audience.
Small sensory moments from Indian life (cutting chai on a Mumbai evening, monsoon on a balcony, a dupatta in the wind).
Longing built by contrast or absence ('tum paas ho to... tum door ho to...').
Soft rhythm: short lines, couplet pairs, a refrain; line breaks matter.
In Hindi, Urdu-influenced words give the register (इश्क़, सुकून, तोहफ़ा, शाम); see lang:urdu_influenced_hindi.
Dashes and ellipses sparingly; at most one exclamation mark; emoji limited to a single heart or flower, if any.
One image per line; the last line lands on a gesture, not a declaration.
cards.sample:
तुम पास हो तो शहर छोटा लगता है,
तुम दूर हो तो एक कमरा भी बड़ा।
इस सालगिरह पर कोई तोहफ़ा नहीं ढूँढ रहा,
बस वही शाम माँग रहा हूँ:
मरीन ड्राइव, दो कटिंग चाय,
और तुम्हारा हाथ मेरे हाथ में।

sources.title: Tone-of-Voice Words (NN/g)
sources.supports: 'Romantic' is one of NN/g's 37 tone words

cards.name: Sarcastic
cards.summary: Says the opposite of what it means, to mock, so it cuts rather than teases. In text it needs context cues or readers take it literally, and it should aim at a situation or institution, never at a vulnerable person.
use_for: meme captions, X posts and reels that mock a shared annoyance (late delivery, traffic, jargon)
satire, parody and sketch or stand-up material
commentary video scripts and political social commentary (with legal care)
critical reviews with a sharp edge
newsjacking posts that react to a familiar absurdity
avoid: Unsignalled sarcasm: in text there is no tone of voice, and the RFC 1855 netiquette warning is that it travels badly. Put the cue in the first line (mock praise, exaggeration, an over-precise number).
Sarcasm in customer support, apologies, health or grief: the reader will take it literally or take offence. Use tone:calm_reassuring or tone:empathetic_supportive.
Aiming it at a person: sarcasm about a named individual can become a defamation question (see the BNS card). Aim at the situation, the system, the habit.
Piling on: more than a few sarcastic lines in a row turn into noise. Break it with a literal line.
Use in translation, subtitles and captions without a cue: it is the register most likely to be read the wrong way.
markers: NN/g position: irreverent and funny (harvest placement); NN/g lists both 'Sarcastic' and 'Snarky' as tone words.
Mock praise as the engine ('Wah, kya baat hai.', 'Bilkul, perfect.', 'Obviously.') followed by the fact that contradicts it.
Exaggeration or an over-precise number that signals the joke ('delivered in 9 days, so quick').
Scare quotes around the thing being mocked ('safe', 'on time').
Short, deadpan sentences; fragments for the turn.
The target is a situation, institution or habit; the reader is on the writer's side.
Ends on a literal sentence that lands the truth.
No emoji needed; if the platform strips tone, add one unmistakable cue instead.
cards.sample: Wah, ₹49 ki delivery sirf 9 din mein pahunch gayi. Itni jaldi? Hum toh Diwali ke baad ki umeed kar rahe the. Parcel ne raaste mein Goa dekha, Jaipur dekha, aur tracking ne bhi chhutti le li. Customer care ne kaha, “Sir, aapka order bilkul safe hai.” Haan, bilkul safe. Bas aapko mil nahi raha.

sources.title: Sarcasm (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: sarcasm is caustic, mocking use of words; it travels badly in text without vocal cues (RFC 1855 warning)

cards.name: Satirical (vyangya)
cards.summary: Exposes hypocrisy and folly through irony, exaggeration and mock-praise; the Hindi tradition is vyangya. It needs a real target and a truth the reader recognises, delivered in plain, straight-faced prose.
use_for: satirical columns and parody pieces in Hindi or English
political and civic satire for social pages and reels (with legal and election-rule checks)
sketch, stage and nukkad-natak material
stand-up writing that mocks institutions and everyday absurdities
short-form scripts and memes built on one exaggerated premise
avoid: Satire with no real target: if nobody is being held to account, it is just a joke. Pick the hypocrisy first, then write.

Naming an individual and asserting facts you cannot prove: use a stock figure ('thekedar ji', 'netaji', 'babu') and a recognisable pattern. Defamation and public-mischief provisions apply (see comp:bns_defamation_speech).
Punching down at the poor, a caste, a religion or a gender: aim at power, pretension and institutions.
Explaining the joke or ending on a rant: the last line must stay in character and straight-faced.
Synthetic or doctored media of real politicians and election-period content without checking the AI-labelling and election-code cards.
markers: NN/g position: irreverent and funny (harvest placement); casual in everyday Hindi, serious in delivery.
Decide before writing: Horatian (gentle, smiling) or Juvenalian (scathing); the choice sets every word.
Mock-praise ('बहुत ईमानदार', 'बड़ा वैज्ञानिक तरीक़ा') that the facts then overturn.
Exaggeration that follows real logic to its absurd end; the reader should be able to say 'that is exactly how it works'.
A straight-faced narrator in plain, everyday prose: Harishankar Parsai, the reference Hindi satirist, wrote plain prose aimed at hypocrisy, corruption and pretence.
Stock characters and recognisable institutions (thekedar, babu, neta, committee) rather than private individuals.
Three-beat build: the claim, the escalation, the absurd conclusion; the punchline is the last clause.
Specific, checkable details (a pothole, a ribbon-cutting, a file moving between tables) that make the target real.
cards.sample: हमारे शहर में सड़क बनाने का तरीक़ा बहुत वैज्ञानिक है। पहले सड़क बनती है, फिर उद्घाटन होता है, फिर पहली बारिश आती है, और गड्ढे इतने गहरे हो जाते हैं कि लोग उनमें अपना भविष्य देख लेते हैं। ठेकेदार जी बहुत ईमानदार हैं। वे हर साल वही सड़क बनाते हैं, ताकि शहर में बेरोज़गारी न फैले।

cards.name: Storyteller / narrative
cards.summary: Carries the message inside a story: a character who wants something, a moment, a turn and a consistent point of view. It is a voice, not a structure; tense, person and scene detail do the work.
use_for: brand stories, about pages and founder posts
case studies and customer stories
personal essays, features and profile pieces
keynotes, TED-style talks and video essays
crowdfunding and fundraising pages
reel, YouTube and podcast scripts that hold attention through a story
avoid: A story with no change: if the character is the same at the end, it is a description. Give the scene a turn ('then', 'but').
Stock characters and openers ('Meet Priya, a busy working mom', 'Once upon a time'): use a specific person, place and time.
A moral at the end: end on an image or an action and let the reader draw the point.
Keeping the product waiting for three paragraphs: the story should reach the product's role early, as the thing that helps with the turn.
Composite or invented customers presented as real: say 'a composite' or use a real, consented story.
markers: A named, specific character with a want in the first lines.
A scene: a place, a time and one sensory detail within the first two sentences.
Consistent point of view (first person for a founder, close third for a customer) and consistent tense; past for a told story, present for immediacy.
One turn: a moment where something changes, marked by 'then', 'but' or a time jump.
Show over tell: actions and objects, not adjectives about feelings.
Dialogue used sparingly, in short lines, in the language the character actually speaks (Hinglish where native).
Sentence length varies: short sentences for the turn, longer ones for scene setting.
Concrete numbers, times and places as proof; the ending is an image or action.
cards.sample: At 4:40 every morning, before the Sadar Bazaar shutters go up, Mohan ji sets a stool outside his shop and counts yesterday's coins. In March, he stopped counting. The boy who sold phone covers next door had screwed a QR code to a steel plate. Mohan ji laughed for a week. In April, he put one up too. The coins are still in the drawer. They are just not his only customers anymore.

sources.title: Storytelling (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: storytelling is increasingly used in advertising to build loyalty; core elements are plot, characters and narrative point of view

cards.name: Technical / precise
cards.summary: Exact, unambiguous, consistent terminology where every sentence can be acted on. Written like a knowledgeable friend: plain, friendly, never cute.
use_for: API references, developer tutorials and READMEs
knowledge-base articles, troubleshooting guides and user manuals
SOPs, technical design docs and release notes
technical blog articles and white papers
error messages that tell the reader exactly what to do
avoid: Using two words for one thing ('workspace', 'project', 'space'): pick one term, define it, keep it. Consistent terms also help non-native readers and translators.
Vague quantities and times ('soon', 'a few minutes', 'large files'): give the number and unit ('within 24 hours', 'files over 25 MB').
'Simply', 'just', 'it's easy': Google's guide flags them as condescending, and they make a failing reader feel stupid.
'Please' in steps and exclamation marks: say 'Click Save.' not 'Please click Save!'.
Idioms, metaphors and jokes: they break in translation and slow the reader. Say the literal thing.
markers: NN/g position (harvest placement): serious, matter-of-fact, respectful; casual-to-neutral formality.
Google's tone guide: conversational, friendly and respectful, like a knowledgeable friend; avoid slang, jargon without need, figurative language.
Second person ('you') and the imperative for steps; present tense; active voice.
One action per step; the condition comes before the action ('If the build fails, run...').
Exact values, units, limits and error codes ('HTTP 401', '24 hours').
UI labels written exactly as on screen, in bold or code format.
One term per concept; acronyms spelled out on first use.
No marketing adjectives, no exclamation marks, no 'please' in instructions.
cards.sample: To rotate the API key, open Settings > Developer > API keys and select Rotate. The old key stays valid for 24 hours. Update every client that uses it before then. Requests that use an expired key return HTTP 401. You can't restore a key after the 24-hour window closes, so copy the new key before you leave this page.

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: voice and tone
sources.supports: conversational, friendly, respectful tone like a knowledgeable friend; avoid jargon, exclamation marks, figurative language, 'please' in steps, and condescending words such as 'simply' and 'it's easy'

cards.name: Tough-love coach
cards.summary: Frank, demanding and on the reader's side: names the excuse, then gives the next step. It is hard on the behaviour, never on the person, and every message ends with an action.
use_for: fitness, career, study and finance-habit creators in short videos and captions
talking-head scripts and motivational talks that confront a stall
nurture emails and newsletters from coaches and educators
LinkedIn and X posts that challenge a common excuse
push notifications and community posts that nudge a lapsed habit
avoid: Shaming the person or their body, income or background: criticise the behaviour ('three months of 'kal se') and keep the reader's dignity.
Harshness with no next step: a lecture is not coaching. Every piece ends with a specific, small, time-boxed action.
Guaranteeing outcomes ('you will crack the exam', 'you will earn Rs 1 lakh'): coaching-sector ads face specific misleading-claim rules (see comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024).
Using it on a reader who is grieving, anxious or in real difficulty: switch to tone:empathetic_supportive.
Fake scarcity to push a sale ('last 3 seats') and 'hustle culture' bravado: the frankness is the draw, not the pressure.
markers: NN/g lists 'Frank' and 'Unapologetic' as tone words; the harvest's placement is serious, casual, mildly irreverent, enthusiastic.
Second person ('tum', 'you') and imperative verbs ('Open the file. Write the first page.').
Names the excuse in the reader's own words ('kal se shuru'), then reframes it in one line.
Short sentences; contractions; Hinglish where the audience speaks it.
Specific numbers from the reader's situation (three months, 20 minutes, 9 pm).
Harsh on the behaviour; no insulting labels (lazy, loser, useless).
Every message ends with one concrete, time-boxed action and an accountability line ('Tell me tomorrow what you wrote').
At most one exclamation mark; energy comes from verbs, not volume.
cards.sample: Teen mahine se tum 'kal se shuru' bol rahe ho. Kal kabhi nahi aata. Tumhe motivation ki kami nahi hai. Tumhe ek 20 minute ka slot chahiye, bina phone ke. Aaj raat 9 baje, 20 minutes, ek hi kaam: pehla page likho. Kharab likho, par likho. Kal subah mujhe batana kya likha.

sources.title: Tone-of-Voice Words (NN/g)
sources.supports: 'Frank' and 'Unapologetic' are NN/g tone words (the coaching pattern itself is practice, not sourced)

cards.name: Urgent
cards.summary: Direct, serious and action-first, used only when time really matters: what to do, by when, and why, in that order. The urgency comes from a real deadline stated plainly, not from capitals or exclamation marks.
use_for: safety alerts, public service announcements and crisis or holding statements
push notifications, SMS and WhatsApp messages about a real deadline (payment due, document expiring, last date to apply)
transactional emails and error messages that block the reader
internal announcements with a deadline and government press notes with a last date
IVR and on-hold messages that must be understood the first time
avoid: Fake scarcity and countdown pressure ('only 2 left', a timer that resets): it is a compliance issue (see comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023) and it destroys trust. Use a real deadline or no urgency at all; see tech:ethical_urgency.
Crying wolf: if every message is urgent, none is. Keep the tone for true deadlines and safety.
Panic words, capitals, exclamation marks and stacked emoji: the NHS manual's model for serious matters is direct, serious and reassuring, not loud.
Burying the action under context: put the action in the first sentence and the reason in the second.
Leaving out the contact: give one channel (number, link, place) for the reader to act on.
markers: NHS service manual model: for serious matters, direct, serious and reassuring.
Action first: the imperative verb in the first three words ('Move to the cyclone shelter before 4 pm.').
Order is what, by when, why; then one contact or next step.
Absolute times and dates ('before 4 pm today', 'by 20 April'), not 'soon' or 'immediately'.
Short sentences, one instruction each; calm verbs (move, call, bring, file).
No capitals for emphasis, no exclamation marks, no emoji; bold only the deadline.
One request per message; one place to act.
Reassurance in one clause where it is true ('The shelter has water and a doctor').
cards.sample: Cyclone alert, Kharoli district. Heavy rain starts at 6 pm today. Move to your nearest cyclone shelter before 4 pm. Take water, medicines, documents and a torch. Do not wait for another alert. The district control room is open now; call the number on your ward notice.

sources.title: NHS digital service manual: Voice and tone
sources.supports: neutral and factual, authoritative but calm and reassuring; serious matters get a direct, serious and reassuring tone; address the reader as 'you'; avoid 'should', which can sound patronising
